name: Helicopter
title: Helicopter (drive train and rotor controls)
intro: This is a light helicopter. Explode it (🧩) to see the turboshaft engine, main gearbox, swashplate and tail rotor. Ask me "How does a helicopter fly forward?"
suggest: How does a helicopter fly forward?
Why does it need a tail rotor?
Open the doors and look inside?

engine.name: Turboshaft engine
engine.info: Compresses air and burns it with fuel so hot gas spins a turbine, sending shaft power forward to the gearbox.

turbine.name: Power turbine
turbine.info: Turbine wheel spun at tens of thousands of rpm by hot combustion gas—the power source for all rotors.

input_shaft.name: Input shaft
input_shaft.info: Delivers high-speed, low-torque rotation from the engine into the main gearbox.

main_gearbox.name: Main gearbox
main_gearbox.info: Steps the engine's tens of thousands of rpm down to a few hundred rpm, multiplying torque many times to turn the main rotor.

bevel_gear.name: Bevel gear and sun gear
bevel_gear.info: A 71-tooth bevel gear turns horizontal input into vertical rotation, driving the sun gear and planetary stage above.

planets.name: Planet gears
planets.info: Orbit the sun gear inside a fixed ring gear for a second stage of speed reduction and torque multiplication.

mast.name: Mast and planet carrier
mast.info: Main rotor shaft rising from the gearbox, turning about 15 times slower than the input shaft with about 15 times the torque.

rotor_hub.name: Rotor hub (teetering)
rotor_hub.info: Central pivot hub that lets one blade flap up as the other flaps down, tilting the whole rotor disc.

blade_1.name: Blade 1
blade_1.info: Airfoil blade. Twisting its leading edge up (increasing pitch angle) pushes more air down to create more lift.

blade_2.name: Blade 2
blade_2.info: Spins together with the other blade and twists along its length to vary blade pitch.

swashplate_lower.name: Lower swashplate (fixed)
swashplate_lower.info: Non-rotating ring held by three servos; it rises, lowers or tilts in any direction to pass pilot commands to the upper plate.

swashplate_upper.name: Upper swashplate (rotating)
swashplate_upper.info: Rides on the lower plate and spins with the rotor, matching the lower plate's height and tilt to twist the blades via pitch links.

pitch_link_1.name: Pitch link 1
pitch_link_1.info: Links the upper swashplate to the blade horn; pushing it up increases the blade's pitch angle.

pitch_link_2.name: Pitch link 2
pitch_link_2.info: Pitch link controlling the second blade's angle.

scissors.name: Scissor link
scissors.info: Hinged drive link that forces the upper swashplate to spin with the mast while letting it slide and tilt freely.

servo_1.name: Servo 1 (front)
servo_1.info: Front hydraulic actuator. Moving all three servos together changes collective lift; moving them differently tilts the swashplate.

servo_2.name: Servo 2 (left rear)
servo_2.info: Left-rear hydraulic actuator working with the other two to raise or tilt the swashplate.

servo_3.name: Servo 3 (right rear)
servo_3.info: Right-rear hydraulic actuator working with the other two to raise or tilt the swashplate.

tail_driveshaft.name: Tail driveshaft
tail_driveshaft.info: Long shaft running through the tail boom from the main gearbox to drive the tail rotor.

tail_gearbox.name: Tail gearbox
tail_gearbox.info: 90° bevel gearbox at the tail that turns driveshaft power sideways to spin the tail rotor.

tail_rotor.name: Tail rotor
tail_rotor.info: Produces sideways thrust to counter main-rotor torque reaction; pressing the pedals changes its pitch to yaw the nose left or right.

cyclic.name: Cyclic stick
cyclic.info: Right-hand control stick. Pushing it tilts the swashplate and rotor disc in that direction to fly forward, back or sideways.

collective.name: Collective lever
collective.info: Left-hand lever. Pulling it up increases pitch on both blades equally, creating more total lift to climb.

pedals.name: Anti-torque pedals
pedals.info: Foot pedals that adjust tail rotor blade pitch to rotate the helicopter's nose left or right.

control_rods.name: Control rods
control_rods.info: Mechanical linkages connecting the cockpit sticks and pedals to the servos and tail rotor.

fuel_tank.name: Fuel tank
fuel_tank.info: Mounted near the centre of gravity so burning fuel doesn't upset the helicopter's balance.

skids.name: Skids
skids.info: Tubular landing skids that are lighter and simpler than wheeled gear.

fuselage.name: Fuselage
fuselage.info: Main cabin structure. Explode (🧩) to reveal the turboshaft engine, gearbox and flight control linkages inside.

canopy.name: Canopy
canopy.info: Large wrap-around clear canopy giving the pilot wide forward and downward visibility.

transmission_cowling.name: Transmission cowling
transmission_cowling.info: Streamlined cover over the main gearbox and lower swashplate to reduce aerodynamic drag.

engine_cowling.name: Engine cowling
engine_cowling.info: Cowling enclosing the turboshaft engine and its rear exhaust outlet.

tail_boom.name: Tail boom
tail_boom.info: Long tail boom housing the tail driveshaft; its length gives the tail rotor a long lever arm to counter torque easily.

tail_fins.name: Tail fins
tail_fins.info: Vertical and horizontal stabilisers that use airflow in forward flight to keep the tail tracking straight.

drives.power: Power (turbine → gearbox → main rotor and tail rotor)

power.title: How the engine turns the rotor

steps.say: Hot gas in the turboshaft engine spins the power turbine at tens of thousands of rpm.
The input shaft feeds power into the main gearbox, where a bevel gear turns horizontal rotation vertical.

quiz.q: The engine turbine spins extremely fast. Why does the main rotor turn so much slower?
options: The main gearbox reduces speed about 15 times to multiply torque
Reducing speed 15-fold multiplies torque 15-fold, giving enough force to turn the heavy rotor blades.
The pilot throttles the engine way down
Turbine engines only run efficiently at high rpm; the gearbox does the slowing down.
Air drag slows it down
The speed ratio between turbine and rotor is mechanically fixed by the gears.

steps.say: Planetary gears reduce speed a second time, turning the rotor mast and both main blades.
Meanwhile, the tail driveshaft taps power from the main gearbox to spin the tail rotor at the back.

quiz.q: What would happen if a single-rotor helicopter took off without a tail rotor?
options: The fuselage would spin uncontrollably in the opposite direction
By action-reaction, turning the main rotor twists the body the opposite way; the tail rotor pushes sideways to cancel that torque.
It couldn't lift off the ground
Lift comes from the main rotor, so it would still rise—while spinning out of control.
Nothing would happen
Unless a helicopter uses twin counter-rotating main rotors, it must have a tail rotor to counter torque.

steps.say: When the pilot pulls up the collective lever, all three servos push the lower swashplate straight up.
The upper swashplate rises with it, and pitch links twist the leading edges of both blades up together.

quiz.q: When you raise the collective lever, how do the two main rotor blades respond?
options: Both blades increase pitch angle together, creating more lift
At constant rotor rpm, steeper blade pitch pushes more air downward so the helicopter climbs.
The rotor spins much faster
Helicopter rotors run at nearly constant rpm; lift is controlled by blade pitch, not speed.
One blade pitches up while the other pitches down
Collective changes both blades equally; unequal pitch across the disc is cyclic control.

steps.say: Higher blade pitch creates more air drag, so the engine automatically adds power to keep rotor rpm constant.
Pushing the cyclic stick forward makes the servos tilt both swashplates forward.
Because the swashplate is tilted, each blade pitches up on one side of its circle and pitches down on the opposite side.

quiz.q: Does the spinning rotor disc reach its highest point at the exact spot where blade pitch is greatest?
options: No, the highest point occurs 90° later in the rotation
Due to gyroscopic precession, a spinning rotor reaches maximum deflection 90° after the force is applied.
Yes, at the exact same spot
Only stationary objects move right where pushed; a spinning rotor responds a quarter turn later.
It peaks on the opposite side
Gyroscopic precession shifts the response by 90°, not 180°.

steps.say: As a result, the entire rotor disc tilts forward, angling the lift vector forward to pull the helicopter ahead.

tail_shaft.title: Broken tail driveshaft
tail_shaft.short: The main rotor turns, the tail rotor has stopped
tail_shaft.symptom: The turbine and main rotor spin normally, but the tail rotor is dead still—meaning the helicopter would spin out in flight. What's broken?
tail_shaft.hint: There is no separate engine in the tail. Check the long shaft between the main gearbox and the tail gearbox.
suspects: The tail rotor blades are broken
tail_shaft.observe: The main gearbox is turning. Follow the inside of the tail boom back: what carries rotation to the tail?
whys: Look closely at the tail—even the tail gearbox and hub aren't spinning, meaning no power is arriving at the tail at all.
Look up top—the turbine and main rotor are spinning at full speed. Power is being lost along the path to the tail.
tail_shaft.cause: The tail driveshaft inside the tail boom snapped, cutting off power from the main gearbox to the tail rotor.
tail_shaft.why: Why does the helicopter fuselage spin uncontrollably when the tail driveshaft breaks and stops the tail rotor?
tail_shaft.answer: Turning the main rotor creates an opposite torque reaction on the body. The tail driveshaft spins the tail rotor to push sideways and cancel that torque; without it, the fuselage spins.
reasons: A broken tail shaft robs the main rotor of lift, causing the spin.
The tail rotor provides forward thrust, so without it the helicopter can only circle in place.
